title: Passions spurned
hookLine: the prince explains why pleasures don't satisfy: fire isn't quenched by fuel (Buddhacarita 11)

cards: Throw a log on a fire and ask it whether it's had enough. It hasn't. It's bigger now, and hungrier.

That's the picture at the center of the prince's answer to King Bimbisara, who has just offered him half a kingdom and a sensible plan for enjoying life in its season. The prince doesn't brush the king off.
He takes the offer seriously enough to give a whole canto of reasons, and the fire is where he begins.

teach.b: First, the respect. Before any argument, the prince honors the king's kindness: it's no surprise, he says in paraphrase, that a man of good family would offer friendship like this, and he's grateful. Second, the fire.
A fire isn't quenched by fuel, and the sea isn't filled by the rivers that run into it. Feed a desire and you don't end it; you make it larger.
Someone who gets what they wanted wants more; someone who gets more fears losing it. Third, the pictures. The poem piles them up.

teach.h: A BONE, A TORCH, A DREAM.
teach.b: Pleasures are like a dog gnawing a dry bone, never fed by it. Like a scrap of meat that birds fight over. Like a torch of straw carried into the wind, which burns the hand that holds it.

Like a dream that's gone when you wake. Like borrowed jewelry that has to be given back. Each says the same thing from a different side: what we reach for to soothe the burning keeps the burning going.
Fourth, the parting. He tells the king he isn't running from enemies or from hardship. He's going after freedom, and he can't be turned aside by a kingdom any more than by threats.
Bimbisara joins his palms, wishes him success, and asks one favor: when you've found what you're seeking, come back and show it to me.
The prince promises. He turns down the passions, not the king. He refuses half a kingdom and keeps a friend.

how: Buddhist teachers use fire as a picture of craving, and in the Pali discourses the Buddha's Fire Sermon describes the senses as burning; in some Buddhist meditation practices people watch a craving rise and fall without acting on it.

o: turning away a friend whose offer insults you
hating the body and all of its wants
turning down pleasures, since feeding desire grows it

games.q: the prince's pictures of pleasure: tap the pairs.
p: a dog with a dry bone
burns the hand that holds it

s: in the poem, the prince insults the king for offering a kingdom
he honors the king's kindness, and they part as friends.
Bimbisara asks the prince to come back once he has found what he seeks
he joins his palms, wishes him well, and asks him to return and show him.
the prince says pleasure is evil
he says it doesn't satisfy: it feeds the want, like fuel feeds fire.

games.q: you're the prince. a king offers you half his kingdom and a plan: pleasure while you're young, wealth in the middle years, religion when you're old. what's your answer?
o: take it, and enjoy each thing in its season.
take it for now, and leave for the forest when you're old.
say pleasure can't be satisfied by feeding it.
games.why: the prince says pleasures feed desire the way fuel feeds a fire, and the sea is never filled by rivers. he turns the kingdom down, and Bimbisara asks him to come back once he has found what he seeks.

practice: Bring to mind one want that keeps coming back however often you feed it, one more thing to buy, a craving for praise, or sugar, or being right, and picture feeding it: does it go quiet, or flare up?
No scolding; just watch the fire. Then, for the rest of the sit, add nothing to it, and see what it does without fuel.

wordCard.voice: Passions spurned. The prince turns down Bimbisara's kingdom, explaining that pleasures feed desire the way fuel feeds fire, and parts from the king as a friend. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: thirst, craving; in Pali, tanha. The want that grows when it's fed.

carryVoice: Your line: fuel doesn't quench fire. The poem ends with a promise to come back. See you tomorrow.
